question: How did Katie Dill explain Stripe’s process for keeping product experiences high-quality across teams?
expected_points: Stripe identified 15 critical user journeys and assigned engineering, product, and design leaders to own their quality.
Leaders regularly walked through journeys as users, logged friction, filed bugs, and scored the experience.
They calibrated scores to build a shared quality bar and improve the end-to-end experience across teams.
evidence_quote: Those 15 things then each have engineering, product and design leaders that are responsible for the quality of those products.

answer.summary: Dill described quality as a shared organizational responsibility, supported by a common vision and alignment, qualitative judgment, and collaborative planning—not a fixed time-allocation formula. She also emphasized showing how quality improvements benefit customers and business outcomes.

sections.heading: Make quality a shared responsibility
sections.content: Quality should not be left to one talented hire, one department, or QA. Stripe relies on people across the organization caring about what they build, keeping the talent bar high, and repeatedly communicating internal standards so they show up in the product experience.

sections.heading: Align teams around a shared vision
sections.content: Even capable people with good taste can make subjective decisions that do not fit together. Dill said teams need vision and alignment, likening product development to building a house: plans, an architect, and a general contractor help ensure the separate pieces form a coherent whole.

sections.heading: Use judgment and collaborative planning
sections.content: For quality scoring, Stripe had settled on a color system rather than a numeric or letter grade. Dill said the assessment is qualitative and based on judgment, avoiding debates over whether something is, for example, a six or a seven. For prioritization, Stripe does not require a fixed formula or percentage of time for quality work: it hires people expected to care about quality, advocates for it at senior levels, and has multidisciplinary teams iterate on plans together, considering whether feature or growth work also improves quality.

sections.heading: Connect improvements to customer and business outcomes
sections.content: Dill cautioned against assuming quality work will not move metrics. For example, customers contacted support because they could not tell how an invoice was performing; a button looked nice but did not clearly show how to access what they needed. Improving it reduced the need to contact support and, she said, improved the bottom line.

Dill said teams need vision and alignment, comparing product development to building a house: plans, an architect, and a general contractor help ensure each component works as part of the whole. [S2]

sections.heading: Build and plan cross-functionally
sections.content: Dill emphasized multidisciplinary people making plans together and iterating on them—considering whether feature or growth work also improves quality. For Stripe’s website, design, engineering, product, and product marketing worked closely; designers and engineers exchanged ideas in rapid cycles to move quickly while maintaining a high standard. [S4, S7]

sections.heading: Use judgment, advocacy, and evidence—not a fixed quota
sections.content: Stripe relied on hiring people with judgment, care, and pride in their work, trusting them to factor quality into decisions, while advocating for quality at the highest levels. Dill said Stripe did not prescribe a formula for how teams divide their time. In discussing quality scoring, she said Stripe had chosen colors rather than numeric scores, because the assessment was qualitative and should draw on people’s judgment. She also stressed showing business impact where possible: clarifying an invoice-status button reduced customers’ need to contact support and improved the bottom line. [S3, S4, S5]
